paragraphs.text: A loose leaf [dark tea](dark:definition) from Guangxi, made in 1970 and sold as Liu Bao. Guangxi on a label [names a region, not a style](guangxi:on-a-label), though a dark tea from the province is most often this one: [Liu Bao](liu-bao:definition), named for the town of Liubao where it began. Like every dark tea, its leaf was piled after it was made so that warmth, moisture and microbes would darken it, then packed and left to age.

At fifty-six years it sits far past the ten that the trade counts as [aged](liu-bao:age-aged), and how it was stored matters as much as how long. Liu Bao this old is [mostly stock](liu-bao:old-stock) that sat in Malaysia or Hong Kong after the mining trade ended. Because such tea is hard to date, the trade reads its age from the basket, the labels and the papers packed with it.

brewing.text: Liu Bao takes very hot or boiling water, because its leaf is dense and gives up its depth slowly. Rinse it once or twice and pour the rinse away. Use about 5 to 8 grams to 100 ml, start with steeps of five to fifteen seconds and add a few seconds each round; a good Liu Bao gives ten cups or more.

notice.text: A deep red, thick cup with woody, herbal and betel nut notes; tea several decades old is often described with ginseng and camphor.
